questions.topic: Ch02 Synthetic Roadblock Incompatible Functional Groups
questions.question: What synthetic roadblock occurs when attempting a nucleophilic addition in Chapter 02 on a substrate containing an unprotected acidic proton?

options.label: A
options.text: The solvent boils away instantly.

options.label: B
options.text: The substrate is converted to an alkane.

options.label: C
options.text: The strong nucleophile acts as a base, undergoing instantaneous acid-base proton transfer rather than the desired nucleophilic addition in Chapter 02.

options.label: D
options.text: The reaction undergoes spontaneous polymerization.

questions.correct_answer: The strong nucleophile acts as a base, undergoing instantaneous acid-base proton transfer rather than the desired nucleophilic addition in Chapter 02.
questions.explanation: Acid-base proton transfer rates are orders of magnitude faster than nucleophilic additions; unprotected acidic groups quench organometallic nucleophiles.

questions.question: In the chemoselectivity decision tree for Chapter 02, which carbonyl is preferentially reduced by sodium borohydride (NaBH₄)?

options.text: Carboxylic acids are reduced first.

options.text: Aldehydes and ketones are selectively reduced in the presence of esters, amides, and carboxylic acids in Chapter 02.

options.text: Amides are reduced first.

options.label: D
options.text: Esters are reduced faster than aldehydes.

questions.correct_answer: Aldehydes and ketones are selectively reduced in the presence of esters, amides, and carboxylic acids in Chapter 02.
questions.explanation: Mild reducing agents (NaBH₄) selectively reduce more electrophilic aldehydes and ketones while leaving less electrophilic esters and amides intact.

questions.question: In the SN1 / SN2 / E1 / E2 decision matrix for Chapter 02, what combination exclusively promotes bimolecular elimination (E2)?

options.label: D
options.text: A primary halide treated with sodium cyanide.

questions.correct_answer: A secondary or tertiary alkyl halide treated with a strong, sterically hindered base (e.g., potassium tert-butoxide, t-BuOK) in Chapter 02.
questions.explanation: Sterically bulky strong bases prevent substitution and exclusively trigger concerted E2 elimination across secondary and tertiary substrates.
